washington-dc.intro: Washington is a planned city, and its trees came with paperwork. The National Park Service keeps a register of witness trees, the Architect of the Capitol records plantings to the year, and the city's own street-tree inventory measures every trunk in its care, which is how its biggest elms, willow oaks and a champion linden reach this map. They join the two original 1912 cherries of the Tidal Basin and a bur oak older than the memorial it shades. Many stand on or near the Mall and Capitol Hill; a few lie across the line in Virginia and Maryland.
washington-dc.meta_description: Washington DC's remarkable trees, from the two original 1912 Tidal Basin cherries and the Grant Memorial bur oak to the city's biggest street elms.
washington-dc.question_meta: The oldest documented tree in central Washington DC is the Grant Memorial Bur Oak on the Capitol grounds. Its story, and the city's other remarkable trees.
washington-dc.question_answer: The oldest tree on our Washington map is the Travilah Oak, a white oak of more than 330 years in Potomac, Maryland, a day trip out of the city. Close behind, by the City of Alexandria's estimate, is a willow oak on the Holmes Run Trail in Alexandria, Virginia, thought to date from around 1707. The oldest documented tree in central Washington DC is the Grant Memorial Bur Oak in Union Square, at the foot of the Capitol, which predates the memorial landscape laid out around it. The city's biggest tree, and possibly its oldest overall, is the champion chestnut oak in Battery Kemble Park.
washington-dc.question_context: Age and documentation are different things in Washington, and the distinction shapes this whole map. Most cities guess at their oldest tree from girth and legend; Washington can often look it up. The Architect of the Capitol has recorded plantings on the Capitol grounds since the Olmsted landscape was laid out, which is how the Grant Memorial Bur Oak's seniority over its own memorial is a matter of record rather than estimate. The National Park Service keeps a formal register of witness trees, from the mulberry that predates the Washington Monument's completion to the elm whose cuttings became the 'Jefferson' cultivar. The city's Urban Forestry Division adds a third layer, an inventory of its street and park trees with a measured trunk for each, which is how a willow oak about 5.4 metres round in a small Ward 7 park, and elms over five metres round in Glover Park and Foxhall, reach this map. Those giants are measured, not dated. None of these trees rivals a European yew for age. What they offer instead is certainty, and a 150-year-old tree with a planting ledger can be a better tree than a 500-year-old one with only a story.

faq_replace.What is the oldest tree in Washington DC: The oldest documented tree in the centre is the Grant Memorial Bur Oak in Union Square on the Capitol grounds. The largest, and possibly older still, is the champion chestnut oak in Battery Kemble Park in the city's northwest. Outside the District, the Travilah Oak in Maryland is put at more than 330 years, and Alexandria's Bicentennial willow oak at around 320.
faq_replace.Are Washington DC's remarkable trees fre: Almost all of them. The trees on the National Mall, the Capitol grounds and the Tidal Basin stand on public federal ground, and the city's giant street trees stand on public sidewalks or in DC parks, visible at any hour. The National Arboretum, Battery Kemble Park, Montrose Park, Dumbarton Oaks Park, Farragut Square and the grounds of Frederick Douglass's house charge nothing to walk in, and Alexandria National Cemetery is open free from sunrise to sunset. Arlington House is free inside a cemetery with its own entry procedure, and Tudor Place's garden asks a suggested donation.

faq_add.q: Where are Washington DC's biggest street trees?
faq_add.a: The city's own tree inventory measures them. The largest willow oak on its park ground stands opposite 6112 Banks Place NE, about 5.4 metres round; American elms of about 5.1 metres grow in Hardy Park and outside 2716 38th Street NW; and the inventory names the linden outside 3819 T Street NW the champion of its genus. The biggest tree in the city overall is still the chestnut oak in Battery Kemble Park.

faq_add.q: Are there remarkable trees in Alexandria, Virginia?
faq_add.a: In the 1970s Alexandria named seventeen Living Witnesses of the American Revolution, and by the city's count two still stand on public land. One is a sweet gum below the flagpole in Alexandria National Cemetery, near King St-Old Town Metro. The other is a willow oak 5.3 metres round on the Holmes Run Trail, which the city dates to around 1707.

leesburg.intro: Leesburg's big trees are measured, not legendary. Loudoun County remeasured its Big Tree Registry in 2025, and four of its trees stand within a hundred metres of each other on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Church in the old town. Among them are a silver linden 6.25 metres round and an Atlantic white cedar, both Virginia champions, and a Japanese chestnut the experts took a while to name. Beyond them are a white oak the town says is older than Leesburg itself, a tulip tree nearly 30 metres tall at Morven Park, and a Shumard oak in Sterling.
leesburg.meta_description: Leesburg, Virginia's remarkable trees, from a white oak older than the 1758 town to the state champion silver linden on the Saint John the Apostle grounds.
leesburg.question_meta: The oldest tree in Leesburg is the Heritage Tree, a white oak in Ida Lee Park the town puts at well over 250 years. Its story, and the town's other trees.
leesburg.question_answer: The oldest tree in Leesburg is the Leesburg Heritage Tree, a white oak beside the Rust Farm House in Ida Lee Park, 50 Ida Lee Drive NW. The town's Tree Commission puts it at well over 250 years, grown from seed before Leesburg was founded in 1758. That age is the town's statement rather than a ring count. The next oldest on our map is the Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park in Sterling, which Loudoun County estimates at about 200 years.
leesburg.question_context: Leesburg's trees are better measured than they are dated. Loudoun County's forester keeps a Big Tree Registry and remeasured it in 2025, so the girth, height and crown of every tree on it are recent and on the record. What the registry does not give is ages. The few that exist come from other voices. The town's Tree Commission says its Heritage Tree grew from an acorn before the town was founded, and the county caption for the Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park puts it at about 200 years, without saying how either figure was reached. So treat the ages on this page as estimates and the measurements as facts. The best walk is short. On the Saint John the Apostle grounds off Church Street NE, a Japanese chestnut and a shellbark hickory stand seven metres apart, with a silver linden and an Atlantic white cedar, both state champions by the county's list, within about a hundred metres. Ida Lee Park and its Heritage Tree are under a kilometre away; Morven Park is a short drive north-west.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Leesburg?
faq.a: The Leesburg Heritage Tree, a white oak beside the Rust Farm House in Ida Lee Park. The town's Tree Commission says it is well over 250 years old and grew from seed before Leesburg was founded in 1758; no ring count has been published.

Four of Loudoun County's registered big trees stand on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church off Church Street NE, within about a hundred metres of each other. The silver linden there, 246 inches round, is the county's Virginia champion for its species. The Shumard oak in Algonkian Regional Park, 109 feet tall, is the tallest on our Leesburg map.

faq.q: Are Leesburg's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Ida Lee Park is a free town park, the Morven Park grounds are free to walk from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily, and the county lists the Saint John the Apostle trees as visible from public property, though it is worth checking for services or funerals before walking onto the church grounds. Algonkian Regional Park may charge for parking at busy times.

faq.q: Can I see Leesburg's trees on foot?
faq.a: The Saint John the Apostle trees and the Heritage Tree in Ida Lee Park are under a kilometre apart in town, and a Loudoun County Transit stop at Union Street and King Street is a few minutes from the church. Morven Park is about 2 km north-west, and Algonkian Regional Park in Sterling is about 25 to 30 minutes east by car.
